definition.question: What is Christian nationalism?
definition.html:
In a widely read definition by an evangelical critic, Christian nationalism is "the belief that the American nation is defined by Christianity, and that the government should take active steps to keep it that way" (Paul D. Miller, Christianity Today, 2021). Stephen Wolfe, whose 2022 book The Case for Christian Nationalism argues for it, summarizes his own view as "a nation that recognizes itself as a Christian people and then wants to act in light of that" (Christ Over All interview, 2023).

The term is contested. Historian Thomas Kidd notes that it "is usually a term of insult" and that far more people apply it to others than embrace it (The Gospel Coalition). See what the surveys show and short answers to common questions.

items.q: What is the difference between Christian nationalism and patriotism?
items.a: Paul D. Miller puts it this way: "Patriotism is the love of country. It is different from nationalism, which is an argument about how to define our country" (Christianity Today, 2021). Thomas Kidd likewise defends a measured Christian patriotism while warning against making America central to redemptive history (The Gospel Coalition).

items.q: How do evangelicals view the label "Christian nationalism"?
items.a: In Pew Research Center's April 2026 survey, 20% of white evangelicals had a favorable view of "Christian nationalism," 18% an unfavorable view, and 38% said they had never heard of it (Pew Research Center). Some writers, including Stephen Wolfe and Doug Wilson, accept the label and argue for it.

items.q: How many evangelicals want Christianity to be the official religion?
items.a: In the same Pew survey, 31% of white evangelicals said the federal government should declare Christianity the official religion of the U.S., 57% said it should promote Christian moral values without doing so, and 10% said it should do neither. Among all U.S. adults the figures were 17%, 43% and 38% (Pew Research Center, 2026). See the chart.

items.q: Why do some surveys say most white evangelicals are Christian nationalists?
items.a: PRRI scores agreement with five statements, such as "U.S. laws should be based on Christian values," and in its 2025 data classed 29% of white evangelical Protestants as Christian nationalism Adherents and 38% as Sympathizers (PRRI, 2026). That measure counts agreement with statements, not views of the label, so it measures something different from Pew's question about the term. See the chart.

items.q: Can Christians want biblical influence on the law without being Christian nationalists?
items.a: Many evangelical critics say yes. Jonathan Leeman separates "Influencers," who want a biblical view of justice to shape the law, from "Identifiers," who want Christianity formally established, and counts himself among the first while urging both to drop the label (9Marks). Kevin DeYoung writes, "I am not a Christian Nationalist, but I almost could be," while rejecting establishment and state coercion in religion (Clearly Reformed).
